segments.title: Radio opening and first question on Mardi Gras Indians
segments.summary: Music plays out and the host opens by asking what the Mardi Gras Indians are.

segments.title: Tribe structure, size and St. Joseph's Night
segments.summary: Cahn describes tribes of 12-15 men with spy boy, flag boy and chiefs, and parades on Mardi Gras Day and St. Joseph's Night.

segments.title: Why Indians? Origins of the tradition
segments.summary: Cahn speculates the tradition began around the turn of the century in black culture, noting Indians were never enslaved; he admits no research exists.

segments.title: Rhythm instruments of the Indians
segments.summary: The Wild Magnolias are heard; Cahn explains tambourine and cowbell, with few drums since the men march all day.

segments.title: Cahn's 1969 recordings and documentary of the White Eagles
segments.summary: A recording of the White Eagles is played; Cahn says he filmed a 30-minute documentary in 1969 following the tribes from New Year's to St. Joseph's Day.

segments.title: Joining a tribe, including the anthropology student Finn
segments.summary: Membership starts in the bar room and is often hereditary; one white Tulane student, Finn, joined the Black Eagles and wrote a paper.

segments.title: African, Haitian and Caribbean roots of the beat
segments.summary: Cahn sees Indian music as a base for New Orleans music, via Africa, Haiti and Santo Domingo; a Paul Oliver Africa field recording is played.

segments.title: Why the Indians do it: ego, following and second line
segments.summary: Cahn calls it a good time and an ego trip with big followings; the sound is a small part of the culture and Indians exist only in New Orleans.

segments.title: Social structure and roles within the tribe
segments.summary: The chief formed the tribe, spy boys are younger, there is a wild man; spy boys scout for other tribes and the flag boy signals.

segments.title: Did the tribes fight? Mardi Gras violence
segments.summary: Asked about fighting and Jelly Roll Morton's account, Cahn recalls Mardi Gras as a day of revenge with shootings and knifings, but cannot verify weapons laws.

segments.title: Costumes then and now, and how long they take
segments.summary: Older costumes were simpler, with turkey feathers; makers dismantle costumes after St. Joseph's Night and start anew.

segments.title: Carnival, Indians and a parade Cahn attended that day
segments.summary: Cahn says tribes would not exist without Carnival and describes a large parade of four groups in matching colors that he watched earlier that day.

segments.title: Professor Longhair's Going to the Mardi Gras
segments.summary: The host plays Professor Longhair's 1949 song and suggests Indian influence on the beat.

segments.title: New Orleans music as a unique blend
segments.summary: Cahn says jazz could only come from New Orleans, blending French martial music, Congo Square, riverfront labor and street vendors.

segments.title: How many tribes exist today
segments.summary: Cahn estimates about 15 tribes now, up from around 12, perhaps fewer than 30 in the past, with new ones forming.

segments.title: Recognition of Indian art, Wild Magnolias and the library exhibit
segments.summary: Cahn credits the Wild Magnolias' record, calls costumes museum pieces, and recalls a librarian who displayed them around 1967 and took heat.

segments.title: Meaning of the chants and Sugar Boy Crawford's Iko Iko
segments.summary: Cahn says the chants are pidgin English he can partly decipher; Sugar Boy Crawford's 1954 Iko Iko is played.

segments.title: Officers' authority, practice nights and bars
segments.summary: Officers have no real power; tribes practice chants on Sunday nights in neighborhood bars, where Cahn met Bo Dollis.

segments.title: Rivalry, cost of costumes and members' incomes
segments.summary: Rivalry is friendly and about costumes worth around $1,000; many members live in the projects with low incomes.

segments.title: Women in the tribes and costume sewing
segments.summary: Some tribes have queens, others exclude women; wives and friends help sew costumes over nine months.

segments.title: The Meters' Two Way Pock-A-Way
segments.summary: A record by the Meters is played and Cahn accepts the modern version while preferring the originals.

segments.title: Future of the Indians and sign-off
segments.summary: Cahn says the Indians or something like them will last forever; the host thanks him and plays Professor Longhair's Big Chief.
